We worked for almost a year trying to generalize the gliding DNA nanotube system to arbitrary DNA origami shapes. Try as we might (controlling the number of motor binding sites, controlling for spurious binding sites on the DNA origami, controlling the geometry of motor binding sites) we could not get any DNA nanostructures other than DNA nanotubes to glide on the glass arrays. These many ahempts and hypotheses about “why DNA origami do not glide” are too numerous to document here. Instead they are documented in the thesis of Dr. Maheo Guareschi [15]. We do not believe that there is any fundamental obstacle to gesng DNA shapes other than DNA tubes to glide, but hypothesize that crypQc protein motor sites in the DNA origami may be prevenQng them from gliding. Solving this would require reengineering the sequence of DNA origami, at a cost of Qme that was beyond what we could accomplish under the current award. Thus we chose to reengineer the DNA nanotube system, and provide control funcQonality that was not present in the system as it was originally developed.
